title: Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames
claim: Tight frames are redundant sets of vectors that span the space evenly, and several different configurations of them exist.
layout: 3 panels side-by-side, 3D vector sketches on grey discs, no text
description: Three side-by-side 3D sketches, each showing five colored arrows radiating from a shared origin in R^3. Each set sits on or around a light-grey elliptical disc with a soft shadow, which gives a sense of depth. The arrows are black, red, blue, green, orange and maroon. In the left panel, four arrows lie roughly in the disc plane and one black arrow points straight up. In the middle panel, the black arrow points down and the maroon arrow points up, with the others spread around the disc. In the right panel, the arrows fan upward in a more clustered, asymmetric pattern. There are no labels, equations or axes. The eye goes first to the tall black or maroon vertical arrows and then to the colored spread. Together the panels show that tight frames of 5 vectors in R^3 can take different shapes.
caption: Examples of tight frames with $k = 5$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategies such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) are effective solutions for fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models; however, their memory requirements scale with the size of the model, $\mathcal{O}(dr)$, where $d$ is the model's hidden dimension and $r$ is the rank. Our proposal, FrameFT, models the parameter update $ÎW$ with a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers, enabling very efficient updates. Only the sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored/optimized, reducing the memory footprint. The sparse structure of the coefficient matrix in FrameFT and the sparsity in the Fusion Frames give large compute benefits, and our analysis provides formal convergence results. We evaluate the idea across a suite of supervised fine-tuning benchmarks, focusing on language tasks, but also report application to vision models. Our experiments show that FrameFT achieves performance on par with/exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques, but needs far fewer trainable parameters.
